title: Pray without ceasing (1 Thessalonians 5:16–18)
hook: always rejoice, pray without ceasing, give thanks in all things

segments.voice: Yesterday, put on mercy, kindness, patience, and above all charity, the bond of perfection. Which virtue did you wear? Day five hundred ninety-three.

It may be the oldest piece of writing in the New Testament. Paul had founded a church in Thessalonica, a port city in northern Greece, and then had to leave in a hurry when trouble broke out. He couldn't go back. So he wrote, probably around the year 50, to a young church he was worried about. Today begins a new stretch, from Thessalonians to Philemon. And near the end of this first letter, Paul packs a whole way of life into three short commands.
screen: `PERHAPS THE OLDEST NEW TESTAMENT BOOK.` → `A CHURCH LEFT IN A HURRY.` → `THREE SHORT COMMANDS.`

segments.voice: "Always rejoice. Pray without ceasing. In all things give thanks; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus concerning you all." Six words in the middle. Pray without ceasing. How could anyone do that? You have to sleep, cook, answer emails. Christians have given several answers. Saint Augustine said the desire of the heart is itself a prayer: if your longing for God never stops, your prayer never stops, even while your lips are busy with something else. Eastern Christians developed the Jesus Prayer, a short line repeated with the breath until it runs underneath everything. A nineteenth-century Russian book, The Way of a Pilgrim, tells of a man who hears this very verse read in church and sets out walking to learn how to do it. The Catholic Church's answer includes the Liturgy of the Hours: psalms and prayers at set times, morning, evening and night, so that the whole day is offered, and the Church as a whole never stops praying. The Angelus bell, rung in many places morning, noon and evening, does the same thing for anyone within earshot. Now look at the third command. In all things give thanks. In, not for. Paul isn't asking anyone to be grateful for cancer or for prison. He's saying there's something to give thanks for even inside a hard thing. He'd know. He was run out of Thessalonica, and he still opens this letter saying he gives thanks for them always. Pray without ceasing, then, isn't nonstop talking. It's a thread that runs through the whole day.
screen: `HOW COULD ANYONE PRAY WITHOUT CEASING?` · `AUGUSTINE: DESIRE IS PRAYER.` · `THE HOURS, THE ANGELUS.` · `IN ALL THINGS, NOT FOR ALL THINGS.` · then, large: `PRAY WITHOUT CEASING.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give thanks inside a hard thing. Settle, and breathe. Think of one hard thing in your life right now. Don't pretend it's good. Just look at it. Now look inside it for one thing you can be thankful for. A person who showed up. Something you learned. A small mercy in the middle of it. When you find it, stay with it. If you pray, you can give thanks for that one thing, right there inside the hard one. If you don't, simply notice that both are true at once. The bell holds the time.
Pray without ceasing. Paul's command to the Thessalonians: not nonstop words, but a thread of prayer running through the whole day. Today's word.
Your line: pray without ceasing. Today, choose one ordinary sound, a door, a notification, a kettle, and let it be a reminder to turn toward God or toward gratitude. Day five hundred ninety-three.

howItsDone: Catholics pray the Liturgy of the Hours at set times of day, and many pray the Angelus at six, noon and six; Catholics also use short repeated prayers, sometimes called aspirations, throughout the day.

original.note: Greek: without interval, without letting up (1 Thessalonians 5:17).

trapdoor: what you thought: an impossible command for monks.
what it means: prayer as a thread through the whole day, and thanks found even inside hard things.
what a scholar hears: adialeiptōs, 'without a gap'; Augustine's desire as prayer; the Liturgy of the Hours sanctifying the day.
